title: Divorce by Mutual Consent — Section 13B HMA

content.overview: Section 13B of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 provides no-fault divorce by mutual consent. Both parties must jointly petition on living separately for one year or more, inability to live together, and mutual agreement to dissolve the marriage. The six-month cooling-off under s. 13B(2) is directory and may be waived. Consent must subsist until the decree.
content.glance: Ask: (1) Joint petition? (2) Living separately ≥1 year? (3) Inability to live together? (4) Free mutual agreement continuing to decree? (5) Cooling-off waiver sought?
content.study:
Section 13B was inserted by the Marriage Laws (Amendment) Act, 1976 as a no-fault consent route.

Sub-section (1): joint petition on living separately for one year or more, inability to live together, and mutual agreement to dissolve.

Sub-section (2): second motion not earlier than six months and not later than eighteen months after first motion; Court passes decree if satisfied of solemnization and truth of averments.

Amardeep Singh v. Harveen Kaur held the six-month period directory and waivable where reconciliation is impossible and further waiting only prolongs agony. Consent must continue until the decree; genuine withdrawal defeats the petition.

Distinct from fault-based s. 13. Case-law verification remains a separate gate.

sections.heading: Scheme and ingredients
sections.body: Joint petition; living separately ≥1 year; inability to live together; mutual agreement; free continuing consent; Court satisfaction after hearing and inquiry.

sections.heading: Two-motion procedure
sections.body: First motion → cooling-off (or waiver) → second motion within the statutory window → decree if conditions satisfied.

sections.heading: Cooling-off period
sections.body: Six months is directory, not mandatory; may be waived when reconciliation is impossible and further delay serves no purpose.

sections.heading: Continuing consent
sections.body: Consent must remain free until the decree. Withdrawal by either party before the decree defeats s. 13B.

sections.heading: Contrast with s. 13
sections.body: s. 13B is no-fault and joint; s. 13 is fault/status and usually unilateral. No proof of matrimonial offence is required under s. 13B.

examples.title: Waiver of cooling-off
examples.body: Long separation, full settlement, free consent — Court may waive remaining cooling-off and grant decree.

examples.title: Withdrawal of consent
examples.body: One party withdraws before second motion — s. 13B fails; contested remedies may remain.

hypotheticals.question: Can the Court decree under s. 13B after one party withdraws consent?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. Continuing free consent is essential; withdrawal defeats the petition.

distinctions.title: s. 13B vs s. 13
distinctions.right: Fault/status ground; usually unilateral; no consent of respondent needed.

misconceptions.trap: Six-month cooling-off is mandatory in every case.
misconceptions.correction: It is directory and may be waived where conditions are met and further waiting is pointless.

misconceptions.trap: A unilateral petition is maintainable under s. 13B.
Consent cannot be withdrawn after the first motion.
misconceptions.correction: Consent must continue until the decree; genuine withdrawal defeats the petition.

cases.name: Amardeep Singh v. Harveen Kaur
cases.facts: Parties sought waiver of the six-month period after long separation and settlement.
cases.issue: Whether the six-month period under s. 13B(2) is mandatory or directory.
cases.ratioDecidendi: The six-month waiting period is directory, not mandatory; the Court may waive it where there is no possibility of reconciliation and further waiting would only prolong agony.
cases.holding: Period held directory and waived on the facts.
cases.relevance: Leading authority on cooling-off waiver; verification gate open.
